Expressionism. An early twentieth-century movement, roughly from nineteen five to nineteen twenty five, that prioritized subjective emotion and inner psychological states over objective reality. Using distorted forms, intense colors, and energetic brushwork to convey feeling, Expressionism emerged from Germany and Austria and produced works of angular discomfort and existential dread that influenced graphic art, sculpture, and film.

Two major groups led the German Expressionist movement. Die Brücke, or The Bridge, and Der Blaue Reiter, or The Blue Rider, were centered in different cities but shared an emotional intensity and formal innovation that defined the era. Edvard Munch's The Scream, though painted in eighteen ninety three before the movement formally coalesced, became the iconic image of Expressionist angst. That swirling, unsettling form expresses psychological disturbance in a way that still resonates today.

The characteristic style was distinctive. Jagged, sometimes crude brushwork, garish colors that clashed intentionally, distorted human anatomy, and dark subject matter exploring anxiety, alienation, sexuality, and urban decay. Artists like Egon Schiele, Oskar Kokoschka, and Emil Nolde created intensely introspective or grotesque figurative work that embraced ugliness as truth rather than seeking beauty.

Expressionist principles extended beyond painting into theater, film like The Cabinet of Doctor Caligari from nineteen twenty, and graphic design. This made it a movement across multiple media, not just canvas and paint.

But the movement faced a catastrophic end. The Nazi regime sharply rejected Expressionism as degenerate in the nineteen thirties. Many works were confiscated or destroyed, and the movement was effectively suppressed by force.
